findings.issue_text: [BUG] The added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, so the 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change' wait never happens and the test only passes (or flakes) by luck of thread scheduling. The test's stated synchronization mechanism does not exist; the assertion after step.join() depends on unwaited background threads, producing flaky CI runs where the flushed message occasionally isn't produced yet.

[BUG] On restart, `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.processes[process_index]` with a new process/thread without stopping the old one when it is a `threading.Thread` (the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard skips the kill entirely for threads), so the old thread keeps flushing the same shards concurrently with the new one. In any `produce_to_pipe` (threaded) deployment where a flusher is restarted via `_ensure_processes_alive`, two threads flush the same shard simultaneously and produce duplicate span segments to Kafka; restarts accumulate leaked threads.

[BUG] The memory backpressure check now calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` once per shard-buffer and sums `used`/`available` across all of them, but `ServiceMemory` from `sentry.processing.backpressure.memory` reports service-level (Redis) memory, not shard-partitioned memory, so the same service's usage is counted once per buffer. With `flusher_processes=N`, `used` is inflated roughly N× relative to `available`, causing spurious `MessageRejected` backpressure at memory levels that were healthy before the change; consumers reject valid span traffic based on fabricated memory pressure.

[BUG] `flusher_processes` from the click option is an unvalidated `int` (default 1, no `min=` bound in click.Option), and a non-positive value like `-1` produces `num_processes = min(-1, len(shards)) = -1`, so `range(-1)` yields an empty `process_to_shards_map` and zero flusher processes are ever created. An operator passing `--flusher-processes -1` (or any negative value) silently gets a consumer with no flusher at all: spans accumulate in Redis unbounded while the consumer reports healthy.

[ADVISORY] `submit()` now invokes `record_stored_segments()` once per shard-buffer (and builds N separate SpansBuffer instances, each constructing its own Redis clients) where the previous code made a single call, turning a previously per-message constant into N Redis round-trips on every submit. The consumer hot path makes `flusher_processes`-multipled Redis calls and connection pools per consumer process, degrading throughput and connection budgets for anyone raising --flusher-processes.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code — no call site in the diff or (per the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards` by index directly) anywhere else — and if it were called it would create a duplicate process for the shard's group without killing the old one. The next maintainer touching restart logic has two near-identical creation entry points, one of which is a restart bug waiting to be wired in; it should be deleted.

[ADVISORY] The metric tag key is inconsistent across the same flusher path: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use tag `"shard"` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses tag `"shards"` for the same shard-tag value. Dashboards/alerts slicing flusher metrics by shard will silently split the wait_produce series into a separate tag dimension, and anyone renaming one key later won't find the other.

[ADVISORY] `if not process: continue` in `_ensure_processes_alive` guards against a value that can never occur — `self.processes` is only populated with freshly started process/thread objects and never with None. Dead branch implies a null-process failure mode that doesn't exist, misleading the next reader auditing restart safety into thinking processes can be missing from the map.

[BUG] join() breaks out of the entire process loop when the deadline expires, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes. With a non-None timeout, once the deadline passes while waiting on process 0, the `break` exits the for-loop so processes 1..N-1 are never waited on and never terminated, leaving orphaned flusher processes holding Redis poll loops and producer resources after consumer shutdown.

[BUG] The wait_produce timer tags the metric with key "shards" while the produce/segment_size metrics use key "shard", silently splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Dashboards/alerts grouping spans.buffer.flusher metrics by the "shard" tag never see spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce, and the new per-shard health monitoring added in this PR cannot correlate produce vs wait times on one axis.

[BUG] When buffer.assigned_shards is empty (e.g., a consumer assigned zero partitions during rebalance), num_processes = min(max_processes, 0) = 0 so no flusher process is ever created and self.processes is empty. A consumer that later gains partitions via rebalance has no flusher process for the newly assigned shards — _ensure_processes_alive iterates an empty dict and returns healthy forever — so segments written to Redis are never flushed to Kafka.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code: it has no caller anywhere in the diff or factory, and it restarts a process without killing or joining the old one. The next maintainer extending health monitoring will find two subtly different restart paths; if the singular one is ever wired up, the un-killed old process keeps polling the same shards, double-producing every segment.

[ADVISORY] No test exercises the multiprocessing (spawn) path: both tests pass produce_to_pipe=messages.append, which forces make_process = threading.Thread, so the new positional `shards` argument and per-shard SpansBuffer pickling through the spawn context is completely unverified. A signature/pickling regression in SpanFlusher.main's spawn invocation (e.g., arg order across the shared Values, or SpansBuffer(shards) not being picklable) ships green CI and only fails in production where produce_to_pipe is None.

[ADVISORY] No test covers the new per-process health monitoring: _ensure_processes_alive's per-process restart counting, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS raising RuntimeError, per-process hang detection via process_healthy_since, and the 'kill then recreate' path are all untested. The regression-prone part of this diff (restart bookkeeping across the new dict-of-processes structure) has zero coverage; a future change that resets process_restarts on restart or reads the wrong process's healthy_since silently disables the consumer-crash safety net in production.

[ADVISORY] The CLAUDE.md isinstance-vs-hasattr documentation snippet is entirely unrelated to the span buffer multiprocess/health-monitoring work described in this PR. Untraceable-to-requirement work lands in the same diff, muddying review and revert scope; a revert of the flusher change would silently lose this unrelated style guidance.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no call site anywhere in the diff or the updated tests. Next maintainer of restart logic must guess which of the two near-duplicate restart helpers is live; the dead one also lacks a restarts counter reset, so a future caller could silently inherit the drift.

[BUG] The wait_produce timer tags the shard list under key "shards" while every other metric in the same function uses key "shard", so the tag schema is inconsistent within one diff. Dashboards/alerts keyed on spans.buffer.flusher.* with tag shard= never match the wait_produce series, so operators slicing flush latency by shard silently miss that metric.

[ADVISORY] max_processes defaults to one process per assigned shard (max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)), so any SpanFlusher constructed without flusher_processes — including the produce_to_pipe/threading test path — spawns N processes, an unbounded process count driven by partition assignment rather than a configured bound. A consumer rebalance to many partitions under the factory default (factory.py passes self.flusher_processes=None when unset) multiplies spawned processes and Redis connections per partition with no operator-configured ceiling; the stated intent is a configurable process limit, and the unconfigured path enforces none.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts constructor internals (process count, shard map) and never submits a message, so the multi-process flush path — per-shard buffer reads, per-process backpressure raise, and restart behavior — has zero end-to-end coverage in this diff. A regression in the multiprocess flush or restart logic (the actual new behavior-bearing logic of this PR) breaks nothing in CI; the first real shard-sharing bug ships to production consumers.

[ADVISORY] join() consumes the shared deadline across processes serially, so with N processes and a finite timeout the total wait is bounded but the per-process remaining_time can go negative and break immediately, terminating still-flushing processes mid-produce. During shutdown with a timeout, later-indexed processes get terminate()d while still draining their Kafka producer futures, losing buffered segments that the single-process version would have flushed.

[BUG] When a flusher running as a threading.Thread (produce_to_pipe path, used by tests and the pipe consumer) is declared hung, _ensure_processes_alive skips killing it but calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shard list, leaving the old hung thread alive alongside a new thread both polling the same Redis shards. Two flusher threads race to fetch-and-delete segments from the same shards, producing duplicate Kafka span payloads or interleaved partial flushes; the hung thread is never reaped, so each hang+restart leaks a live thread and multiplies Redis load.

[BUG] submit() now fans out one buffer.get_memory_info() Redis round-trip per flusher process (default max_processes = len(assigned_shards), one process per shard) on every message, where the previous code made a single call. The memory-backpressure check becomes an N-way external-call fan-out on the hottest path of the consumer (called on every submit), multiplying Redis load by the shard count (potentially dozens) even though every per-shard buffer reports the same service memory data, inflating latency and COGS with no accuracy gain.

[BUG] _create_process_for_shard(shard) is dead code with no caller anywhere in the diff, and if ever invoked it would restart the owning process but never remove the killed process from self.processes before re-registering, doubling an entry's work. The next maintainer calling this helper during shard-level recovery gets an unbounded process leak (each call spawns a new process for the same shards) instead of the intended single restart; delete it or route it through the same replace logic as _ensure_processes_alive.

[ADVISORY] The two timers use inconsistent tag keys for the same shard identity: metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag}) vs metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag}). Dashboards and alerts grouping flusher latency by shard tag silently split into two tag namespaces, so per-shard produce vs wait-produce comparisons never join; also the comma-joined shard list (e.g. "1,3") has unbounded cardinality as shard assignments change, degrading metric index performance.

[ADVISORY] join() breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires, so every SpawnProcess later in the dict iteration order is never sent terminate(), and is only reaped because it is daemon=True. During a timeout-limited shutdown, some flusher processes keep running and keep producing to Kafka after join() returns, letting in-flight segments race against the next consumer instance's rebalance; the old single-process code had the same window but the multi-process version widens it to N processes non-deterministically.

[ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats an explicit 0 (or the CLI passing 0) as "use one process per shard", inverting the operator's intent to disable parallel flushers. An operator setting --flusher-processes=0 to force the single-process behavior instead gets the maximum fan-out (one process per shard), the exact opposite of the requested configuration.

[BUG] Aggregating `get_memory_info()` across one SpansBuffer per process silently redefines the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` option's semantics: available (and used) memory is counted once per flusher process because every shard buffer reads the same Redis service memory. With N flusher processes, `available` is summed N times while used also scales, so the effective threshold the option enforces changes with process count — an operator setting max-memory-percentage=0.8 with 4 processes gets a ~4x looser/tighter gate than the option value they accepted; the previously-calibrated backpressure threshold drifts without any option change or human sign-off.

[ADVISORY] Removing the public `self.buffer` attribute (replaced by `self.buffers: dict[int, SpansBuffer]`) is a silent breaking change to SpanFlusher's external surface: the factory still constructs and passes a single `buffer`, and the flusher discards it in favor of per-shard clones, so any out-of-tree caller (tests, tooling, subclass) that reads `flusher.buffer` now hits AttributeError. Existing callers/tests referencing `flusher.buffer` or assuming the flusher flushes via the buffer instance the factory passed break at runtime; the factory-passed buffer and the flusher's shard buffers also drift apart, making which buffer actually holds the Redis state ambiguous to the next maintainer.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is dead code: no call site anywhere in the diff or existing code invokes it; its docstring even says 'restart that process' but restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly. A future maintainer calling it during a restart will double-spawn a process for those shards (the old entry in self.processes is overwritten but never killed), leaking a live flusher that competes for the same Redis segments; the dead method invites that misuse and should be deleted.

[ADVISORY] The new metric tags use inconsistent keys — `"spans.buffer.flusher.produce"` and `segment_size_bytes` get `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` while `wait_produce` gets `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` — and the shard tag is a joined comma list, creating unbounded tag cardinality across deployments with varying shard counts. Anyone building dashboards/alerts on flusher latency must query two different tag keys for the same process's metrics, and the per-shard-list tag value explodes metric series cardinality (one series per distinct shard-set combination, which changes on every restart or rebalance), degrading metrics performance and breaking existing saved queries keyed on the untagged metric names.

[ADVISORY] In `join`, when the shared deadline expires mid-loop, `break` skips both waiting on and `terminate()`-ing all remaining flusher processes, so only the first process is reliably terminated on timeout. A consumer shutdown that hits its join timeout leaves N-1 spawned flusher processes alive holding Redis segment leases; they keep flushing and producing after the consumer is considered down, so operations teams see ghost producers during any timed-out deploy or crash-loop restart.

[BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` 'to give flusher threads time' is a no-op because the test itself monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top of `test_basic`. The comment's claimed wait never happens; whatever race between the drift change and the flusher threads the sleep was meant to mask remains, so the test passes (or flakes) for the original timing reason and the added line provides false confidence that the race was fixed.

[BUG] test_flusher_processes_limit is a mirror-of-implementation structure test: it asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and shard-map totals, but never submits a message, never produces a Kafka payload, and never asserts any flushed output, so the new multi-process flush data path (shard-subset SpansBuffers, per-process produce, tag-tagged metrics) is never exercised end-to-end. A regression where the 2-process flusher silently produces nothing (e.g. shard buffers not wired to the segments the consumer writes, or flushed segments lost because record_stored_segments runs on the wrong buffers) passes this test green; I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and test_flusher.py and neither drives a message through a multi-process flusher.

[BUG] The rewritten health-monitoring path in `_ensure_processes_alive` — per-process restart counting, kill of a hung process, the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, and the `_create_process_for_shards` restart call — has no test that triggers it: neither tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py nor test_consumer.py kills a process or advances `process_healthy_since` past `max-unhealthy-seconds`. Defects in the restart logic ship undetected — e.g. the new `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill guard means a hung threading.Thread is never killed but `process_restarts` is still incremented and the process is 'recreated', so a thread hang loop or an over-eager consumer restart in production has zero test coverage; the previous single-process kill/restart behavior was equally untested and this diff makes the code more branchy, not safer.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten backpressure assertion `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` only checks that at least one process saw backpressure, weakening the old single-value check. In a multi-process configuration, a bug where backpressure detection is broken for all but one shard's process (e.g. the wrong Value handle passed to some process during restart) passes this test; with the single-process default it degenerates to the old assertion, so the gap only bites when flusher_processes > 1 — exactly the configuration this PR introduces and which no functional test covers.

[BUG] When the flusher runs in threading mode (produce_to_pipe is set, i.e. the test/pipeline path) and a process is judged unhealthy by the hang check, _ensure_processes_alive never terminates the old thread (the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`) yet immediately calls _create_process_for_shards to start a new thread over the same shards. Two concurrent flushers poll the same Redis shards and produce the same segments to Kafka twice, duplicating span data downstream; the zombie thread also keeps updating the shared healthy_since value, masking future hangs of the replacement thread.

[BUG] SpanFlusher.join() uses `break` inside the per-process loop to exit the entire outer for-loop when the deadline is exhausted, so all remaining processes are never terminated or waited on. On a timeout during consumer shutdown, flusher processes for later process indices keep running and keep producing spans to Kafka after join() returns, so messages are emitted for offsets already committed (or not committed) by the dying consumer, producing out-of-order/duplicate data with no bounded shutdown.

[ADVISORY] The new --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, and flusher.py computes `max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 (or any falsy value) silently means one-per-shard rather than unlimited-parallel or an error. An operator setting --flusher-processes=0 expecting to disable the extra processes instead gets maximum process count spawned (one per shard), multiplying Redis connections and memory usage per consumer; the falsy-or idiom makes the CLI value ambiguous.

[ADVISORY] Each per-shard-group flusher process gets its own SpansBuffer instance (self.buffers), and submit() now calls record_stored_segments() and get_memory_info() on every buffer on every submit, replacing the previous single-buffer calls. With N processes the consumer performs N Redis round-trips per submit for record_stored_segments plus N more for the memory check, an N-fold hot-path increase in Redis traffic per message batch; a shard owner debugging slow ingestion sees the consumer's Redis QPS scale with flusher_processes even though shard ownership was supposed to partition the work.

[BUG] All flusher processes share a single `current_drift` multiprocessing.Value with last-write-wins semantics, so the drift/clock bookkeeping the committer relies on is now racy across processes. A fast process that finishes flushing advances current_drift while a slow process's shards still have unflushed segments in Redis; the committer treats drift as global progress and can commit offsets before those spans are produced to Kafka, so a consumer crash after commit permanently drops the slow shards' buffered spans.

[BUG] On an unhealthy process, `_ensure_processes_alive` calls process.kill() and immediately starts a replacement via `_create_process_for_shards`, without joining or reaping the killed process. For a `cause="hang"` restart the old process is still running during the new one's startup; both processes poll the same shards concurrently, and if a segment fetch is not strictly atomic per shard, segments get produced to Kafka twice (duplicate spans downstream), while the unreaped zombie accumulates one dead process object per restart.

[ADVISORY] `join()` consumes the shared deadline sequentially per process and `break`s out without terminating the remaining processes when time runs out. With N flusher processes and a bounded timeout, the first hung process eats the entire deadline; every later process is skipped without terminate() and its Redis-backed segments are never flushed before the consumer exits — operators doing bounded shutdowns see silently unflushed spans for all shards after the first stuck one.

[ADVISORY] The `wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` while every other metric in the same loop uses tag key `"shard"`. Whoever builds dashboards on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`/`segment_size_bytes` (tagged `shard`) gets `wait_produce` split into a disjoint series set under `shards`, so per-shard latency panels silently miss the produce-wait metric entirely.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent on every call — initial creation and every restart — and the old buffer object in `self.buffers[process_index]` is replaced with no cleanup. Each restart leaks the previous buffer's Redis clients/connection pools in the long-lived consumer process, and with many shards/processes the parent now holds N independent Redis client setups on the submit() path (record_stored_segments, get_memory_info) where previously one buffer served it — connection count and per-submit Redis round-trips scale with flusher process count.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly, so this method has no caller. The next maintainer editing restart logic via the singularly-named helper (the natural entry point given its name) changes nothing, and drift between the two near-identical methods makes the restart path riskier to modify.

[ADVISORY] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses truthiness on an int option, so `flusher_processes=0` falls back to one-process-per-shard instead of being honored or rejected. An operator who sets `--flusher-processes 0` intending to minimize processes (or a misconfigured deploy) silently gets the maximum process fan-out, the opposite of the intent, with no warning.

[ADVISORY] The max-memory check now sums `get_memory_info()` across all per-shard buffers on every submit() call when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` is below 1.0. If each per-process SpansBuffer's get_memory_info reports the same backing services, `used` and `available` are multiplied by the process count (ratio coincidentally preserved but metrics/logic fragile to per-shard service sets), and submit() issues N remote service-memory lookups per message where it previously issued one — a hot-path latency regression on every ingested span when the option is enabled.

adjudication.rationale: In the threaded mode (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), `_create_process_for_shards` creates a `threading.Thread` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. When `_ensure_processes_alive` decides a restart is needed, it only attempts `process.kill()` if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so threads are never stopped. It then calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, which starts a new thread for the same `shards` while the old thread can still be alive (the shared `self.stopped` flag is not set during restart). This can lead to concurrent flushing for the same shards and duplicated production, and leaked threads across repeated restarts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Removing the public `self.buffer` attribute (replaced by `self.buffers: dict[int, SpansBuffer]`) is a silent breaking change to SpanFlusher's external surface: the factory still constructs and passes a single `buffer`, and the flusher discards it in favor of per-shard clones, so any out-of-tree caller (tests, tooling, subclass) that reads `flusher.buffer` now hits AttributeError. Existing callers/tests referencing `flusher.buffer` or assuming the flusher flushes via the buffer instance the factory passed break at runtime; the factory-passed buffer and the flusher's shard buffers also drift apart, making which buffer actually holds the Redis state ambiguous to the next maintainer.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a concrete external-surface change: `SpanFlusher.__init__` no longer assigns `self.buffer = buffer` (it now builds per-shard `SpansBuffer` instances and stores them in `self.buffers`, and all uses switch to iterating `self.buffers.values()`). Any code that previously accessed `flusher.buffer` will now raise `AttributeError`, and the original `buffer` passed by the factory is not retained on the instance. That’s a real, diff-grounded compatibility/API concern, but not a provable functional defect within this PR since all in-tree call sites/tests shown are updated to the new fields.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is dead code: no call site anywhere in the diff or existing code invokes it; its docstring even says 'restart that process' but restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly. A future maintainer calling it during a restart will double-spawn a process for those shards (the old entry in self.processes is overwritten but never killed), leaking a live flusher that competes for the same Redis segments; the dead method invites that misuse and should be deleted.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is introduced but there is no visible call site added that invokes it; all restart logic shown goes through `_ensure_processes_alive()` which directly calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. The method also does not terminate/kill any existing process before calling `_create_process_for_shards`, so if it were used in the future it could indeed spawn an additional process/thread for the same shard group while overwriting `self.processes[process_index]`, potentially leaving the prior worker running. This is a diff-grounded maintainability hazard rather than a currently-triggered defect (dead/unused code in the shown changes).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new metric tags use inconsistent keys — `"spans.buffer.flusher.produce"` and `segment_size_bytes` get `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` while `wait_produce` gets `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` — and the shard tag is a joined comma list, creating unbounded tag cardinality across deployments with varying shard counts. Anyone building dashboards/alerts on flusher latency must query two different tag keys for the same process's metrics, and the per-shard-list tag value explodes metric series cardinality (one series per distinct shard-set combination, which changes on every restart or rebalance), degrading metrics performance and breaking existing saved queries keyed on the untagged metric names.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces inconsistent metric tag keys: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})` versus `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` in `SpanFlusher.main` (flusher.py). It also sets `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))`, meaning the tag value encodes a list of shards per process, which can create many distinct tag values depending on shard assignment/rebalances. This is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/metrics-quality issue rather than a correctness defect in the flusher’s behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In `join`, when the shared deadline expires mid-loop, `break` skips both waiting on and `terminate()`-ing all remaining flusher processes, so only the first process is reliably terminated on timeout. A consumer shutdown that hits its join timeout leaves N-1 spawned flusher processes alive holding Redis segment leases; they keep flushing and producing after the consumer is considered down, so operations teams see ghost producers during any timed-out deploy or crash-loop restart.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join`, the loop over `self.processes` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before reaching later processes, which skips both waiting on and the subsequent `process.terminate()` for all remaining processes. Even if the deadline expires while waiting on an earlier process, that process is terminated, but any processes after it may not be terminated at all due to the `break` (see `for process_index, process in self.processes.items(): ... if remaining_time <= 0: break ... if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` 'to give flusher threads time' is a no-op because the test itself monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top of `test_basic`. The comment's claimed wait never happens; whatever race between the drift change and the flusher threads the sleep was meant to mask remains, so the test passes (or flakes) for the original timing reason and the added line provides false confidence that the race was fixed.
matched_golden_ids: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate points out that `time.sleep(0.1)` is ineffective because `time.sleep` was monkeypatched to a no-op in the test, so the intended wait for flusher threads never happens—same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_flusher_processes_limit is a mirror-of-implementation structure test: it asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and shard-map totals, but never submits a message, never produces a Kafka payload, and never asserts any flushed output, so the new multi-process flush data path (shard-subset SpansBuffers, per-process produce, tag-tagged metrics) is never exercised end-to-end. A regression where the 2-process flusher silently produces nothing (e.g. shard buffers not wired to the segments the consumer writes, or flushed segments lost because record_stored_segments runs on the wrong buffers) passes this test green; I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and test_flusher.py and neither drives a message through a multi-process flusher.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `test_flusher_processes_limit` (added in `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py`) only asserts internal implementation details (`len(flusher.processes)`, `flusher.max_processes`, `flusher.num_processes`, and shard distribution via `process_to_shards_map`) and then calls `step.join()` without ever submitting messages to the strategy, producing any `KafkaPayload`, or asserting any flushed output. From the diff, the multi-process behavior involves creating per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances and calling `record_stored_segments()` / `get_memory_info()` on `self.buffers.values()`; a wiring regression could plausibly occur without being caught by this test. This is a test-quality / coverage concern, not a directly verifiable functional bug in runtime behavior from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rewritten health-monitoring path in `_ensure_processes_alive` — per-process restart counting, kill of a hung process, the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, and the `_create_process_for_shards` restart call — has no test that triggers it: neither tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py nor test_consumer.py kills a process or advances `process_healthy_since` past `max-unhealthy-seconds`. Defects in the restart logic ship undetected — e.g. the new `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill guard means a hung threading.Thread is never killed but `process_restarts` is still incremented and the process is 'recreated', so a thread hang loop or an over-eager consumer restart in production has zero test coverage; the previous single-process kill/restart behavior was equally untested and this diff makes the code more branchy, not safer.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces significantly more branchy restart/health-monitoring logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive` (per-process `process_healthy_since`, `process_restarts`, conditional `kill()` only for `multiprocessing.Process`, and `_create_process_for_shards` restarts). The added/modified tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and the updated `test_flusher`) only cover shard/process mapping and backpressure-state plumbing; none advance `process_healthy_since` past `spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds` or simulate a dead/hung process/thread to exercise the restart/RuntimeError paths. This is a concrete, diff-grounded gap in test coverage for newly expanded logic rather than a directly provable functional bug from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rewritten backpressure assertion `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` only checks that at least one process saw backpressure, weakening the old single-value check. In a multi-process configuration, a bug where backpressure detection is broken for all but one shard's process (e.g. the wrong Value handle passed to some process during restart) passes this test; with the single-process default it degenerates to the old assertion, so the gap only bites when flusher_processes > 1 — exactly the configuration this PR introduces and which no functional test covers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `SpanFlusher` from a single `backpressure_since` Value to per-process Values (`self.process_backpressure_since`), and updates the test from `assert flusher.backpressure_since.value` to `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`. That does weaken the guarantee compared to asserting every process/shard path sets backpressure, and the PR introduces new multi-process sharding/restart wiring (`_create_process_for_shards` passing `self.process_backpressure_since[process_index]`) that is not directly functionally exercised beyond process-count/shard-distribution checks. This is a concrete test/coverage gap tied to the new multi-process logic, not a proven correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When the flusher runs in threading mode (produce_to_pipe is set, i.e. the test/pipeline path) and a process is judged unhealthy by the hang check, _ensure_processes_alive never terminates the old thread (the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`) yet immediately calls _create_process_for_shards to start a new thread over the same shards. Two concurrent flushers poll the same Redis shards and produce the same segments to Kafka twice, duplicating span data downstream; the zombie thread also keeps updating the shared healthy_since value, masking future hangs of the replacement thread.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher is unhealthy it restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, but termination is only attempted under `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()`. In threading mode (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), the flusher worker is a `threading.Thread` (created in `_create_process_for_shards`), so the old thread is never stopped before a new thread is started for the same `shards`. Both threads will run `SpanFlusher.main(shard_buffer, shards, ...)` polling/producing for the same shard set, risking duplicate Kafka production. Additionally, both old and new threads share the same `self.process_healthy_since[process_index]` multiprocessing.Value passed as `healthy_since`, so the old thread can continue updating it and mask hangs in the replacement thread, as described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] SpanFlusher.join() uses `break` inside the per-process loop to exit the entire outer for-loop when the deadline is exhausted, so all remaining processes are never terminated or waited on. On a timeout during consumer shutdown, flusher processes for later process indices keep running and keep producing spans to Kafka after join() returns, so messages are emitted for offsets already committed (or not committed) by the dying consumer, producing out-of-order/duplicate data with no bounded shutdown.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` contains `if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which exits the entire outer loop when the overall deadline is exhausted. That means any later processes in the dict are neither waited on nor terminated (`process.terminate()` is only reached for processes iterated). With the new multi-process design (`self.processes` dict), this can leave some flusher processes still alive after `join()` returns on timeout, unlike the previous single-process implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, and flusher.py computes `max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 (or any falsy value) silently means one-per-shard rather than unlimited-parallel or an error. An operator setting --flusher-processes=0 expecting to disable the extra processes instead gets maximum process count spawned (one per shard), multiplying Redis connections and memory usage per consumer; the falsy-or idiom makes the CLI value ambiguous.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a CLI option `--flusher-processes` (default=1) and threads it into `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)`. In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the new line `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats an explicit `0` (or other falsy int) the same as “unset”, resulting in `max_processes` becoming `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. That means `--flusher-processes=0` silently spawns one process per shard (via `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`) rather than honoring the operator’s explicit 0 value or rejecting it, which is an incorrect/ambiguous behavior directly introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Each per-shard-group flusher process gets its own SpansBuffer instance (self.buffers), and submit() now calls record_stored_segments() and get_memory_info() on every buffer on every submit, replacing the previous single-buffer calls. With N processes the consumer performs N Redis round-trips per submit for record_stored_segments plus N more for the memory check, an N-fold hot-path increase in Redis traffic per message batch; a shard owner debugging slow ingestion sees the consumer's Redis QPS scale with flusher_processes even though shard ownership was supposed to partition the work.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.__init__, the diff introduces per-process shard buffers (self.buffers populated in _create_process_for_shards with `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` and stored via `self.buffers[process_index] = shard_buffer`). In submit(), the code now loops over `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` instead of a single `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()`, and similarly aggregates memory info by iterating over all buffers (`for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`). This is verifiably an O(num_processes) increase in these calls per submit compared to the prior single-buffer behavior, which can translate into increased Redis traffic if those methods touch Redis (as implied by surrounding comments about Redis backpressure/memory). It’s a concrete performance/architecture concern introduced by the change, not a correctness defect that can be proven broken from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] All flusher processes share a single `current_drift` multiprocessing.Value with last-write-wins semantics, so the drift/clock bookkeeping the committer relies on is now racy across processes. A fast process that finishes flushing advances current_drift while a slow process's shards still have unflushed segments in Redis; the committer treats drift as global progress and can commit offsets before those spans are produced to Kafka, so a consumer crash after commit permanently drops the slow shards' buffered spans.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce multiple flusher worker processes/threads, but `SpanFlusher` still creates a single `self.current_drift = mp_context.Value("i", 0)` and passes that same shared `current_drift` into every worker via `_create_process_for_shards(... args=(..., self.current_drift, ...))`. So the “single Value shared across processes with last-write-wins semantics” part is directly grounded in the diff. However, the claimed consequence (committer using `current_drift` as a global progress signal leading to committing offsets before all shards’ spans are produced, causing data loss) cannot be verified from this diff because no committer/offset logic using `current_drift` is shown here. This is still a concrete review concern created by the change (per-process bookkeeping mixed with a global drift value).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] On an unhealthy process, `_ensure_processes_alive` calls process.kill() and immediately starts a replacement via `_create_process_for_shards`, without joining or reaping the killed process. For a `cause="hang"` restart the old process is still running during the new one's startup; both processes poll the same shards concurrently, and if a segment fetch is not strictly atomic per shard, segments get produced to Kafka twice (duplicate spans downstream), while the unreaped zombie accumulates one dead process object per restart.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is unhealthy it unconditionally calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` after (attempting) a kill, but it never `join()`s/reaps the old worker. Worse, the kill path only runs for `multiprocessing.Process` (`if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()`), so in the thread-backed mode (`produce_to_pipe is not None`, where `make_process = threading.Thread`) a `cause="hang"` restart will start a new thread without stopping the old one, leaving both threads polling/producing for the same shard set concurrently. Even for process-backed mode, lack of `join()` means killed processes can remain unreaped (zombies) and the old process may overlap briefly with the replacement during startup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `join()` consumes the shared deadline sequentially per process and `break`s out without terminating the remaining processes when time runs out. With N flusher processes and a bounded timeout, the first hung process eats the entire deadline; every later process is skipped without terminate() and its Redis-backed segments are never flushed before the consumer exits — operators doing bounded shutdowns see silently unflushed spans for all shards after the first stuck one.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.join(), a single shared `deadline` is used for all processes, but the loop does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before reaching later processes. Those skipped processes never hit the `while process.is_alive()` wait nor the subsequent `process.terminate()` call, so a bounded timeout can leave some flusher processes running (or later killed as daemons) without an orderly shutdown. This behavior is directly visible in the new join() implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `wait_produce` timer uses tag key `"shards"` while every other metric in the same loop uses tag key `"shard"`. Whoever builds dashboards on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`/`segment_size_bytes` (tagged `shard`) gets `wait_produce` split into a disjoint series set under `shards`, so per-shard latency panels silently miss the produce-wait metric entirely.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, metrics in the flush loop use inconsistent tag keys: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})`, but `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses `"shards"`. This is a concrete, diff-verifiable observability issue that will split series and break per-shard dashboards/queries expecting `shard`, but it doesn’t change the functional correctness of flushing itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent on every call — initial creation and every restart — and the old buffer object in `self.buffers[process_index]` is replaced with no cleanup. Each restart leaks the previous buffer's Redis clients/connection pools in the long-lived consumer process, and with many shards/processes the parent now holds N independent Redis client setups on the submit() path (record_stored_segments, get_memory_info) where previously one buffer served it — connection count and per-submit Redis round-trips scale with flusher process count.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `_create_process_for_shards` creates a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each time and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]` (and uses all `self.buffers.values()` on the parent submit-path for `record_stored_segments()` / `get_memory_info()`). On restart, `_create_process_for_shards` is called again and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]` without any explicit cleanup of the previous buffer object. The claim that this definitively leaks Redis clients/connection pools is not directly verifiable from the diff (SpansBuffer internals aren’t shown), but the resource/perf concern introduced by per-process buffers and overwriting without cleanup is real and grounded in the changed code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly, so this method has no caller. The next maintainer editing restart logic via the singularly-named helper (the natural entry point given its name) changes nothing, and drift between the two near-identical methods makes the restart path riskier to modify.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is defined but the shown code paths never call it. Process creation uses `_create_processes()` -> `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, and restarts in `_ensure_processes_alive()` also call `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. No other caller appears in the diff, so the singular helper is effectively dead/unreferenced and could mislead maintainers or drift from the actual restart logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses truthiness on an int option, so `flusher_processes=0` falls back to one-process-per-shard instead of being honored or rejected. An operator who sets `--flusher-processes 0` intending to minimize processes (or a misconfigured deploy) silently gets the maximum process fan-out, the opposite of the intent, with no warning.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats `0` as falsy. Since the new CLI option `--flusher-processes` is `type=int` with no validation/min bound, an operator can pass `0`, which will then silently fall back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and maximize process fan-out. This is directly verifiable from the diff: `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` forwards `flusher_processes` into `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)` and `SpanFlusher` uses `or` to compute the effective limit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The max-memory check now sums `get_memory_info()` across all per-shard buffers on every submit() call when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` is below 1.0. If each per-process SpansBuffer's get_memory_info reports the same backing services, `used` and `available` are multiplied by the process count (ratio coincidentally preserved but metrics/logic fragile to per-shard service sets), and submit() issues N remote service-memory lookups per message where it previously issued one — a hot-path latency regression on every ingested span when the option is enabled.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit()`, the max-memory check changed from a single `memory_infos = list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())` call to iterating all per-process buffers and doing `memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` for each (`for buffer in self.buffers.values(): ...`). This is diff-verifiable and means the memory-info collection work now scales with the number of flusher buffers/processes whenever `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`. The finding’s concern about duplicated service-memory entries (and thus summing `used`/`available` multiple times) is plausible given the code now blindly aggregates across buffers, though whether they report identical backing services isn’t provable from the diff. The hot-path extra calls/latency risk is a concrete review issue, but it’s not a correctness defect by itself.
